title: Malta, Rome, and the Unhindered Word
summary: The shipwrecked company lands on Malta, where Paul survives a viper's bite and heals the father of the island's chief official and many others. After three months they sail on to Italy, and believers come out along the road to welcome Paul to Rome. Under guard in his own lodging, Paul meets the Jewish leaders of the city, some are persuaded and others refuse, and for two years he proclaims the kingdom of God and teaches about Jesus boldly and without hindrance.
story: This is the end of Acts and the goal of its second half. Jesus told his followers they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth (1:8), and the Lord told Paul he must testify in Rome (23:11). Now the prisoner arrives in the capital of the world. Luke does not tell us the outcome of Paul's trial or how he died. He ends instead with the gospel being preached in Rome, openly, by a man in chains. The story that began with a small group waiting in Jerusalem closes with the message about Jesus at the center of the empire, and the reader is left to see that the word has outrun every attempt to stop it.
historical:
Malta, which Luke calls Melite, lies south of Sicily. Tradition places the wreck at the inlet now called St. Paul's Bay on the island's northeast coast, and the soundings and features Luke describes are consistent with that area, though other locations have been proposed. Luke calls Publius the first man of the island, and inscriptions from Malta use a similar title for its leading official, a small detail that fits the place. After three months, in the early spring, the company sails on another Alexandrian grain ship through Syracuse in Sicily and Rhegium at the toe of Italy to Puteoli on the Bay of Naples, the main port where the grain fleet unloaded. From there Paul travels overland on the Appian Way. The Forum of Appius and Three Taverns were stopping points on that road, roughly forty and thirty miles from Rome.

The arrival is usually dated about AD 60 to 62, in the reign of Nero. Paul lived under a form of house arrest, chained to a soldier but in rented lodging, able to receive visitors. Many scholars place the so-called prison letters (Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon) in this period, though some argue for Caesarea or Ephesus instead. Why Acts ends here is debated. Some think Luke wrote before the trial was decided; others think he ended deliberately with the gospel's arrival in Rome, knowing his readers knew the rest. Early Christian tradition holds that Paul was eventually executed in Rome under Nero, and many believe he was first released and traveled further, as the Pastoral Letters may suggest.
cultural:
Luke calls the islanders barbaroi, the Greek word for people who did not speak Greek; it is not an insult here, since Luke praises their extraordinary kindness. Their reaction to the viper reflects popular belief. They assume Justice, whom Greeks personified as a goddess (Dike), has caught up with a murderer who escaped the sea; when nothing happens, they swing to the opposite conclusion that Paul is a god, much as the crowd at Lystra did (Acts 14:11-18). Luke records both judgments without comment and lets the healings that follow speak for themselves. The ship's figurehead, the Twin Brothers, was Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus in Greek myth and popular patrons of sailors.

Roman custody came in degrees, from prison cells to military custody in a private house. Paul's was of the lighter kind, and the fact that he lived in his own rented quarters suggests he met the cost himself or with help from believers. His first act in Rome is to call the Jewish leaders, following his lifelong pattern of going to the Jew first (Romans 1:16). Their answer, that no letters had come from Judea, may reflect the difficulty of winter travel or a decision by the Jerusalem authorities not to pursue the case in Rome.
literary: The chapter has three movements: Malta (verses 1-10), the road to Rome (verses 11-16), and Paul's meetings with the Roman Jews (verses 17-31). The last movement closes the book with a scene that sums up its pattern: Paul reasons from the Law and the Prophets, some believe, some refuse, and he turns to the Gentiles. He quotes Isaiah 6:9-10, the words given to Isaiah at his commissioning about a people who hear without understanding, which Jesus also quoted about his parables (Luke 8:10) and which other New Testament writers use to explain why many in Israel did not believe. The book's final word in Greek is an adverb meaning unhindered. Luke ends not with Paul's fate but with the word of God at large in Rome.

outline.t: Welcome on Malta and the viper
Publius's father and the sick of the island healed
Paul meets the Jewish leaders in Rome
The kingdom of God, divided response, and Isaiah's words

doctrines.note: Acts begins with Jesus speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3) and ends with Paul proclaiming it (28:31). The kingdom is God's reign, now centered on the Lord Jesus Christ, announced in the capital of Caesar's empire.
The gospel reaches Rome, fulfilling the pattern of Acts 1:8. Paul still goes to the Jew first, then declares that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, who will listen.
A shipwreck, a winter on Malta, and a prisoner's chain all become the route by which God brings the gospel to Rome. The chain does not stop the word; it gives Paul an audience.

words.note: Akolutos, without hindrance, freely. It is the last word of Acts in Greek. A related verb (koluo, to hinder) appears at key moments in the book, as when the Ethiopian official asks what prevents him from being baptized (8:36) and Peter asks who could forbid water for Cornelius's household (10:47). The book ends by saying nothing hindered the word.

Parresia, boldness or freedom of speech, originally the citizen's right to speak openly in the assembly. Acts uses it repeatedly for the apostles' preaching (4:13, 4:29, 4:31). A prisoner under guard speaks with the freedom of a citizen.
Basileia, kingdom, reign. It frames the book (1:3, 28:23, 28:31). In Rome, where Caesar's reign was celebrated everywhere, Paul announces another kingdom and teaches about another Lord.

Dike, justice or penalty; here the islanders' goddess Justice, who they assumed had caught Paul. Luke reports their belief without endorsing it, and the story overturns it: Paul is not a murderer and not a god, but a servant of the God who heals.

christ: The last sentence of Acts names the whole subject of the book: the kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus Christ. Luke's two volumes began with the birth of Jesus in the days of Caesar Augustus (Luke 2:1) and end with Jesus proclaimed as Lord in Caesar's own city. Paul's healing of Publius's father, with prayer and laying on of hands, recalls Jesus healing Peter's mother-in-law of a fever (Luke 4:38-39); the risen Lord continues his work through his servants. The Isaiah passage Paul quotes is the same one Jesus used, so that the response to Paul in Rome repeats the response to Jesus in Galilee. And the chained witness who speaks freely shows the shape of Christ's kingdom, which advances not by force but by testimony.

hard.q: Does the end of Acts mean God has given up on the Jewish people?
hard.a:
Paul's closing words, quoting Isaiah and announcing that salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, have sometimes been read as a final rejection of Israel, and that reading has fed Christian contempt for Jews in later centuries. The text itself is more careful. Paul calls the Roman Jews brothers, says he has no charge against his nation, and describes his chain as worn for the hope of Israel (verse 20). Some of his hearers are persuaded (verse 24), as Jews have been throughout Acts, and the book's first believers were all Jewish.

Interpreters differ on how final the scene is. Some read it as Luke's closing verdict that the mission to Israel as a whole has ended and the future lies with the Gentiles. Others note that Paul has turned to the Gentiles twice before (13:46, 18:6) and still gone first to the synagogue in the next city, and that he welcomes all who come to him in verse 30, which would include Jews. Paul's own letter to this city insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2). Isaiah's words, in their first setting, were a prophet's grief over his own people, spoken from inside Israel, not a verdict from outside it.

questions: The islanders judged Paul first a murderer and then a god. How quickly do you draw conclusions about people from what happens to them?
Acts ends before telling us what happened to Paul. Why might Luke have chosen to end with the gospel preached rather than with Paul's fate?
Paul spoke boldly while chained to a guard. What limitations in your life might be places where God still intends to use you?
